differences.title: 1. PRIMARY TARGET
differences.leftDesc: vLLM is designed specifically for high-throughput transformer inference, optimizing token generation and batching across concurrent requests using continuous batching and memory-aware scheduling.
differences.rightDesc: TorchServe is a general PyTorch model serving framework, wrapping models behind HTTP/gRPC handlers. It focuses on standard deployment workflows, preprocessing/postprocessing, and multi-model endpoints.

differences.title: 2. MEMORY MANAGEMENT
differences.leftDesc: vLLM uses a paged attention KV cache, allocating GPU memory in blocks so variable-length sequences don’t fragment VRAM. KV blocks can be reused as requests finish or extend.
differences.rightDesc: TorchServe relies on the model’s native tensor allocations and PyTorch runtime memory behavior. KV cache strategies are not built-in; you manage caching logic inside your model or handler.

differences.title: 3. BATCHING STRATEGY
differences.leftDesc: vLLM continuously batches active sequences at the token level, interleaving decoding work from different prompts. This keeps GPUs busy during generation and reduces tail latency.
differences.rightDesc: TorchServe typically batches at the handler level via custom batching utilities; generation workflows often remain request-scoped. Unless you implement token-level interleaving, batches don’t naturally align with decoding.

differences.title: 4. DECODING WORKFLOW
differences.leftDesc: vLLM’s engine exposes knobs for generation-time optimization (e.g., decoding parameters and acceleration paths), making it straightforward to integrate multi-step decoding behaviors for faster throughput.
differences.rightDesc: TorchServe can serve any PyTorch generation code you provide, but it doesn’t include an LLM-specific decoding engine. Token-by-token loops remain in your model, not the server scheduler.

differences.title: 5. PERFORMANCE OBSERVABILITY
differences.leftDesc: vLLM provides runtime signals tied to LLM scheduling: queueing, token throughput, cache hit/block behavior, and scheduler decisions. These metrics map directly to why latency/throughput changed.
differences.rightDesc: TorchServe offers server-level logs/metrics, but deeper LLM performance (tokens/sec by stage, KV cache efficiency) depends on how you instrument your handler/model. Engine-level causality is limited.

differences.title: 6. SCALING MODEL
differences.leftDesc: vLLM is commonly scaled by deploying GPU workers tuned for LLM parallelism. Its scheduler packs many concurrent generations onto one or more GPUs efficiently using shared KV handling.
differences.rightDesc: TorchServe scales via multiple replicas (often containers) behind a load balancer. Each replica runs its own model instance and caching behavior, so packing efficiency across replicas is coarse.

differences.title: 7. DEPLOYMENT CONSTRAINTS
differences.leftDesc: vLLM requires an LLM-optimized stack (CUDA kernels, attention/KV mechanisms, and supported transformer formats). You get strong performance but with narrower assumptions than generic model servers.
differences.rightDesc: TorchServe depends on TorchServe infrastructure and PyTorch model artifacts. It’s flexible for custom architectures, but LLM-specific performance (KV paging, token-level scheduling) is not automatic.
